ours.name: Standard Scramble
ours.approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (Easy Pass Trail, North Cascades National Park, backcountry permit required for camping). The trail climbs steadily through forest, crossing Easy Pass Creek three times, and breaks out into subalpine meadows and heather benches before the final push to Easy Pass at about 6,550 ft — roughly 3.5-3.6 miles and 2,700-2,800 ft of gain, typically 2-3 hours. Steep snow can linger on this stretch well into July, and an ice axe is recommended; the tread can be hard to follow across snowfields, and the meadows are fragile, so stay on trail/rock where possible. From the pass, leave the high traverse and descend the Fisher Creek side: the trail
ours.descent: This is a scramble, not a technical rock route, and no rappels are used — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-4 upper section back to the saddle (accounts vary on the exact character here: some parties describe a short, fun class 2-3 scramble from a notch just below the true summit; others describe roughly 250 vertical feet of class 3-4 terrain near the top

fktText: Description "Ragged Ridge" is a coveted link-up in the Washington mountaineering community. Many "light and fast" enthusiasts test their mettle to see if they can complete the entire ridge of 4 peaks within daylight hours. Not all succeed. Just finishing car-to-car in a day is a feather in the cap of any mountain athlete. On loose, steep terrain these 21 miles, with mixed 3rd and 4th class climbing to gain summits, are a real test piece. These are not for the casual runner. This is not forgiving terrain. Experience with exposure, loose rock, scrambling and route finding are an absolute pre-requisite for an attempt on this ridge. Starting and finishing at Easy Pass Trailhead , there are 4 required high points on the traverse - Mesachie (8795') , Katsuk (8680') , Kimtah (8600') , and Cosho (8332') - they may be tagged in any order, so long as all are tagged before returning to the car. (GPS + photos on true summits for substantiation) After all four peaks are tagged, there are the options of returning on the high traverse of ledges/steep terrain or dropping to the easy pass trail below, both of which involve steep technical terrain. In his blog, Sean O'Rourke lays claim to having completed this link up in 14hrs car-to-car and he certainly has the resume to back up that kind of claim on this type of terrain . In my opinion, it should be considered the time to beat for Ragged Ridge As far as times with GPS substantiation for us young-guns where GPS'ing everything is the norm, Jas

ours.name: East Ridge
ours.approach: From the PCT North Trailhead at I-90 Exit 52 (~3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail north through Commonwealth Basin and up onto the Kendall Ridge switchbacks. At roughly 5.5-5.7 miles you reach the Kendall Katwalk, the exposed rock traverse blasted into the cliff band that most parties use as a progress checkpoint. Continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel/Alaska Lake — the last reliable water before the high basin and ridge — for another 0.3-2 miles to the base of Bumblebee Pass. A short, steep, unmaintained climbers' path (loose tread, care warranted with a pack) climbs to the 5,400 ft pass, then drops down the north side into the open basin directly below Mount Thomson's south face
ours.descent: Descent reverses the East Ridge line back to the 5,600 ft notch and down into the basin, then back up and over Bumblebee Pass to rejoin the PCT for the hike out. On the ridge itself, established rappel stations exist at up to three short steps, marked by fixed/fresh webbing and rappel rings threaded on rock horns (not bolted). fktText: Description https://www.outdoorproject.com/adventures/washington/climbing/mount-thompson-west-ridge For the aspiring mountaineer, Mount Thomson provides a convenient introduction to alpine climbing. Its east ridge is mostly a walk-up with a short fourth-class section at the very end. Its west ridge provides a bit more of a challenge with five or so pitches of low fifth-class climbing. While many climbers bemoan the "long" approach, it is easy. Several miles of walking on the well-graded and maintained Pacific Crest Trail is all you need to get there. A short but steep climber's path leaves the PCT just as it traverses above Alaska Lake. This path ascends to Bumblebee Pass, where you'll get the first good views of the mountain if the weather is good. Crossing a rock-strewn alpine basin to the talus on the other side puts you face to face with Mount Thomson's distinct profile. The technical climbing begins at a small notch just before the terrain gets vertical. The first two pitches are meandering and somewhat vertical, ending at the bottom of a broad slab. After the slab, there is a bit more vertical climbing to the false summit. A dirty trail leads down from the false summit to a belay notch, where the final pitch of climbing begins. A few quick moves lead to the true summit. While the climbing is not technically demanding, you'll encounter a great deal of exposure, some loose and dirty spots, and some route finding challenges. Bring a light rack of cams sized to 3 inches in

ours.name: Gorillas Direct
ours.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls. For the Cascadian Couloir and South Headwall, turn right onto the Longs Pass Trail at the junction about 1.7 miles in, climb to Longs Pass (about 6,250 ft) near mile 2.9, and descend the rocky climbers' trail on the far side to Ingalls Creek, cross on a log bridge, and follow the climbers' path up the meadow into the base of the Cascadian Couloir (South Headwall lies further up-basin via the same drainage). For West Ridge, the North Ridge routes, and the West Face Wall (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), instead stay on the Ingalls Way Trail ov
ours.descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend via the main gully with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right on a large bench with a single-rope rappel option, before reaching Stuart Pass bivy sites.

fktText: Description "Without a rival as the crown peak in the central Cascades of Washington, Mount Stuart has been pronounced the single greatest mass of exposed granite in the United States...its northern and eastern faces are the alpine climax of the Wenatchee Mountains. They make a powerful impact on first sight...The mountaineering problems are magnified by the mountain's massive dimensions and its complexity." - excerpted from Fred Beckey's "Cascade Alpine Guide" Overlooking the Kittitas Valley and visible from many other nearby mountains, Mt. Stuart is an icon of Central Washington. Sitting at 9,415ft, this beautiful mountain attracts many climbers during the summer months. The primary FKT route starts at the Ingalls Lake trailhead, goes up and over Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, and ascends the Cascadian Couloir to the summit. Descent is by the same route. https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/routes-places/ingalls-stuart-area-review/mt-stuart-cascadian-couloir The West Ridge is the second most commonly climbed route on the mountain. It includes low fifth class climbing, a great deal of scrambling, and significant route-finding challenges. ours.name: Standard Scramble (off the PCT)
ours.approach: From I-90 Exit 52 (West Snoqualmie Pass), the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT northbound) lot sits just off the exit ramp on a short dirt spur (Northwest Forest Pass required; the ~50-car lot fills early on weekends). From the trailhead (~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north through second-growth forest: a first switchback at 0.6 mi (3,230 ft), a switchback pair at 1.5 mi (3,690 ft), and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at 2.0 mi (3,830 ft), where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases downhill slightly to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 mi (3,775 ft) - stay right/straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two
ours.descent: Descend the same way you climbed: back down the loose dirt-and-talus boot path to the stump on the PCT, then follow the PCT south/back roughly 5.5-6 miles to the Exit 52 trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no technical rappelling anywhere on the standard route (rappels: 0). ours.name: King Kong - Gorillas Direct Direct
ours.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3), then continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge, and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft). The West Face Wall, home to the Gorillas routes (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek.
ours.descent: Quickest descent follows the main gully of the West Ridge via scrambling and downclimbing before breaking skier's right onto a large bench with a single-rope rappel option, then downclimbing to bivy sites at Stuart Pass.

ours.name: Daniel Glacier / Southeast Slopes
ours.approach: From the Cathedral Rock/Deception Pass trailhead at the end of FR-4330 (elev. ~3400 ft), start on Cathedral Rock Trail #1345 (not the Deception Pass Trail #1376, which leaves the north end of the same lot), which climbs steadily through forest. At about 2 miles, pass the signed junction with Trail Creek Trail #1332 and continue straight; the main trail passes Squaw Lake shortly after. The trail continues climbing for roughly two more miles, breaking out of trees into subalpine meadows and switchbacks, and tops out at Cathedral Pass (~5,600 ft, roughly 4.2-4.5 miles in) at a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. From the pass, drop briefly toward Deep Lake on the PCT; at a switchback partway
ours.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit area, downclimb the loose scree/talus band beside the Daniel Glacier remnant back to the 7600 ft saddle below the East Summit, then retrace the climbers' trail traversing scree beneath the East Summit back onto the crest of the Southeast Ridge. From there, drop the braided boot paths back down through talus and heather to Peggy's Pond -- in ear

fktText: Description Mount Daniel is the high point of King County, WA, and a frequently climbed mountain. The standard Southeast Ridge route begins at the Cathedral Pass Trailhead. Follow the Cathedral Pass trail for approximately 4.2 miles to it's junction with the PCT. Take the PCT southbound for about two tenths of a mile to the junction of Peggy's Pond trail. Follow this trail to Peggy's Pond then ascend the climbers trail on the SE Ridge of Mount Daniel. Follow this obvious ridge to the saddle below the East Peak of Mount Daniel and then traverse over to the West Peak and true summit of Mount Daniel. The majority of the route is class two or one with perhaps a few class 3 moves. Trailhead to summit is just shy of eight miles. ours.name: Mount Pilchuck Trail (Standard Route)
ours.approach: From Granite Falls, follow WA-92 east and then the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 10-11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile past Verlot, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right (south) onto Mount Pilchuck Road (FR 42). Follow FR 42 for about 6.8 miles — rough, washboarded gravel for the first ~4.7 miles and paved for the last ~1.9, with the gravel's condition varying by year — to the Mount Pilchuck Trailhead parking area (roughly 3,000-3,100 ft). In years when FR 42 is gated below the trailhead (common in shoulder season), the hike instead starts from the Heather Lake Trailhead, adding roughly 5 miles and substantial elevation gain each way.
ours.descent: From the lookout, reverse the short ladder and boulder-field scramble, then follow the marked trail (orange blazes across the open boulder field, then single-track through forest) back down to the trailhead parking area. Do not attempt to shortcut down the old ski-area clearing visible west of the trail — it looks like a shortcut but is steep and brushy, and has contributed to lost-hiker rescues.

fktText: Description The sentinel of Everett, Mt Pilchuck is the closest peak to the suburban area and is a popular hiking destination in the summer months. It even has a lookout on the summit with great views of the surrounding mountains and the Puget Sound. Route starts at the trailhead -- ascent ends at/in the lookout, roundtrip goes up to the lookout and back down to the trailhead. current FKTs are as follows: Men's round trip: 1:05:25 by Ben Rauk Women's round trip: 1:36:44 by Peyton Colee Men's ascent: 33:20 by Dan Kraft Women's ascent: 45:25 by Claire DeVoe (supported) GPS Track pilchuck.gpx 38.79 KB FKTs roundtrip ascent Images Log in or register to post comments Comments aelwell Wed, 01/15/2025 - 04:05pm If looking for more vert, an alternative route starting at the Mt Loop Highway and ascending the gravel road provides 4125 ft elevation gain and 19 miles round-trip. This also eliminates driving up the slow and rough access road to the trailhead. ours.name: Sulphide Glacier
ours.approach: From the end of FS Road 1152-014 (~2,500 ft), the route starts on the Shannon Ridge Trail #742, an old roadbed heading northeast. Follow it about 2 miles to where the road tread gives out around 3,800 ft, then continue on the true trail, angling left through brush onto the open ridge crest. Roughly 0.75 mile farther (~4,600 ft) the trail reaches timberline, where continuous snow often persists into midsummer (crampons/axe are worth carrying above this point in early season). From timberline, follow the broad, undulating ridge crest through meadows and broken timber for about 2 more miles to a pass where a major north-south ridge is met (~5,400 ft) — the Sulphide Glacier and the summit pyrami
ours.descent: Descend the same line: reverse the Sulphide Glacier back to camp, then the Shannon Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Off the summit, the standard descent down the central gully of the summit pyramid is a mix of downclimbing and rappelling. NPS climbing rangers have reported parties periodically replacing worn rap rings and anchors in the gully, so expect a mix of fixed rings/webbing at establishe

fktText: Description https://www.mountaineers.org/explore/routes-places/mt-shuksan-sulphide-glacier A 7 mile forest approach to a gentle glacier climb in the North Cascades that ends with a 500 feet snow (early season) or rock scramble up the summit pyramid. Impressive views of Mount Baker and the North Cascade peaks. If the summit rock is icy, evaluate carefully and perhaps forgo summit. Times: 5-6 hr hike to camp, and 5-6 hr from camp to summit. ours.name: Monitor Ridge
ours.approach: From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead (3,700 ft, the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain, reached via FR-90/FR-83/FR-81/FR-830 from Cougar), the route starts on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. This trail climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline at roughly 4,800 ft — the last shade and the last practical spot to filter water (a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail; nothing reliable higher up, so most parties carry all water from the car). At timberline the trail ends and the route transitions onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash. From he
ours.descent: Descent is the same Monitor Ridge line back to timberline and then the Ptarmigan Trail back to Climbers Bivouac — there is no rappelling on this route (0 rappels; it is entirely a walk-off/scramble descent). The critical descent hazard is at the top: the crater rim is corniced with wind-built overhanging snow/ice that has repeatedly broken away, including a fatal collapse and multiple large rim fa

fktText: Description Mt St Helens (8365') is unusual in that it is basically a "new" mountain since the 1980 eruption which removed 1312' feet from its height. summitpost.org lists 3 main routes, Butte Camp , Worm Flows / Swift Glacier , and Monitor Ridge (shown on the map below). The latter 2 routes have attracted FKT activity. You must go to the true summit to count! Just going to the crater rim isn't enough. Another challenge on St Helens that has become popular is as follows: Starting from climbers bivouac, summit Mt. St. Helens via Monitor Ridge. Descend and run either clockwise or counterclockwise around the entire Loowit trail. Summit a second time via Monitor ridge and finish back at climbers bivouac. The initial idea was to get in a sunrise and then a sunset summit in one day, and the Loowit was the time to space out the two summits. It has been an informal quasi-event for a few years. ours.name: Cascadian Couloir
ours.approach: Drive to the Esmeralda (DeRoux Campground/Teanaway) trailhead at the end of North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), elevation ~4,243 ft — from I-90 exit 85 near Cle Elum, take SR 970 northeast, then Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking. From the trailhead, hike an old mining road/climbers' trail about 0.25 mile to a fork and take the right (east) branch toward Longs Pass. The trail climbs a mostly open, sun-exposed hillside — worth starting before dawn in summer to avoid the heat — gaining roughly 2,000 ft over about 2 miles to Longs Pass (~6,250 ft), the high point of the approach and the first place Mount Stuart and the Cascadian Couloir come into view.
